content.thinking:
I'm thinking through proportions for the whimsical capybara design—a rounded barrel body, blocky head, tiny ears and legs—keeping it cheerful while loosely grounded in real capybara size, with a small perched bird for scale and charm.

Now I'm planning the skeleton: a hip root with a spine chain to the chest, short neck and head with jaw and ear joints, four legs each with shoulder/elbow/wrist/toe joints (capybara-accurate toe counts), a tiny tail stub, and a separate bird skeleton with body, wings, tail, legs, and beak joints sitting atop the head.

For the look, I'm settling on warm brown-ochre fur with painted grain and mottling, a lighter belly, darker nose and rump, pink inner ears and blush cheeks, glossy sphere eyes with highlights, and a cheerful bluebird companion wearing a tiny leaf hat for a playful story detail.

I'm also considering tucking a small blossom behind the capybara's ear, a blade of grass in its mouth, and whimsical touches like fur tufts, whiskers, and freckle dots to round out the character without overcomplicating things.

Now I'm working out exact coordinates in meters, sketching a roughly 1.1m capybara body-plus-head with exaggerated proportions, and defining the spine chain points from the hips through to the chest.

I'm continuing to lay out the skeleton: naming the spine joints, adding a short stubby tail chain, a neck chain connecting chest to head, and starting the head and jaw joints with the elongated blunt capybara snout shape.

For the head geometry, I'm lofting the cranium from the head joint through several stations—widening from the skull down to a tall, blunt, squarish muzzle to capture the whimsical exaggerated capybara nose shape.

Now I'm adding details: a dark ellipsoid nose pad with nostrils at the front, a lower jaw swept as a capsule shape below the joint, and a simple draped smile line on the head's surface to give it a friendly whimsical expression. Next I'll move on to the eyes.

For the eyes, I'm placing small dark spheres with white highlight dots on the upper sides of the head, topped with flattened fur-colored "eyelid" spheres covering the upper half to give that sleepy, content capybara look. Then I'll add tiny rounded ears near the top-back of the head using flattened spheres with pink inner coloring, hinged with joints, and finally position a little bird sitting at the top of the head between the ears.

I'm setting up the bird as its own chubby jointed figure with a body, head, upper and lower beak, wings, tail, and legs, facing roughly forward with its head tilted slightly for charm, then moving on to sketch out the capybara's short front legs starting from the shoulder joints.

Planning leg IK chains...

Totaling 14 toe joints works within budget. For hind legs I'm placing roots further back, using a two-segment thigh-to-ankle structure bent to roughly match standing height, then attaching feet similarly, with a thicker thigh bulge for the capybara's whimsical proportions.

For the body I'm lofting a barrel shape along the spine from rump to chest using six width/height stations that bulge in the middle and taper at both ends, keeping the belly about 0.14m above ground so the legs peek out visibly below.

Checking proportions, the body comes out a bit too tall relative to the head, so I'm scaling it down to a 0.42 height centered around y=0.33, giving a top around 0.54 and bottom around 0.12, with shoulder and hip joints nestled inside at y=0.26 and 0.30, and keeping the mid-body width at 0.50.

Now sizing the head for extra whimsy — bumping it up to 0.28 tall and 0.27 wide with oversized eyes, placed at y=0.40 from z=0.30 to 0.66, roughly level with the back so it doesn't awkwardly poke above the body line, and noting there's no visible neck, just a direct joint connection.

I'm working out whether to add a short neck chain linking the chest to the head joint, deciding the overlap between the neck and body loft is fine since the oversized head will cover any seam — leaning toward keeping a simple neck chain for rigging purposes while letting the body loft stop around z=0.30 and the head geometry pick up from there.

Now I'm reconsidering how the bone list feeds the loft: the spine and hips chains need to connect properly, but if the hips joint and the first spine joint share the same position, that bone effectively has zero length, which could cause issues in the loft calculation — I need to make sure the hips joint has some actual offset so the bone chain works correctly.

I'm reconsidering ownership of the rump region — rather than giving it to a tail chain, I'll keep it owned by hips, with hips as a distinct point at (0,0.33,-0.40) and the spine chain starting from that same hips point going forward, following the standard root-and-chain pattern.

Let me try repositioning the hips further back and running the spine chain forward from there with four spans, but then the hind legs need their own parent point near the pelvis rather than way back at the hips location — I'm adjusting coordinates to resolve that mismatch.

Now I'm working out a short tail chain going backward from the hips for the rump, and planning to use a bone definition listing tail, hips, spine as one continuous loft path (since chains can run either direction), with the hind leg joints named following the hip-knee-ankle convention and parented at the hips.

For the mirrored front/back limbs, I'm deciding to use raw world x-coordinates with a side multiplier (+1 for left, -1 for right) rather than relying on local s-values, naming joints with L/R suffixes. For fur, I'm layering a countershade paint over a mottled base for the belly contrast, then nesting a grain paint on top along the z-axis to create streak texture.

Now I'm working through texel density for the fur texture — estimating body surface area around 3m² to figure out whether 1024 or 2048 resolution gives fine enough detail, leaning toward sticking with 1024 to keep the budget light while checking if it's still crisp enough, before moving on to placing fur tufts on the cheeks.

I'm planning tuft card placement across cheeks, chest, rump, brow, and ear fringe, designing each tuft as a simple pointed SVG shape in grayscale so it can be tinted by the coat paint when rendered on the card root — letting the fur cards pick up the body's actual coloring automatically. Then I'm sketching out the detail list: coat paint for the body with a lighter belly, dark mottled spots on the back, and a darker spine stripe built from layered countershading.

For the head, I'm redoing a slightly redder coat tone, a lighter muzzle, a dark brownish-purple nose pad with nostrils, light whisker-pad bulges with whisker dots, six thin whisker sweeps per side, and a lighter cream chin. For the eyes I'm adding lids and eyebrow tufts, plus a custom paint function that blends pink blush into the head coat based on distance from cheek-center points, mixing colors when within radius. I'm also planning small rounded ears with pink interiors and tufts, and I'm about to work out the teeth.

For the teeth, I'm going whimsical: two small cream buck-teeth poking just below the nose pad over the lower jaw for a cute look. I'm then shaping tapered legs with darker gradient lower portions, toe nubs with dark claws, and ankle fur tufts, plus a small furry tail stub. Finally I'm adding a pink daisy made of petal extrudes behind the left ear, and considering a blade of grass in the mouth for extra charm.

Now I'm adding a thin curved reed poking from the left mouth corner with a tiny seed head, making sure it aligns naturally with the capybara's jaw. Next I'm designing a bluebird companion—blue back, orange breast, white belly—with a sphere head, big eyes, orange-yellow beak, folded wing sweeps, a three-feather fan tail, thin pale legs with toes, and a small crest tuft.

I'm placing the bird perched between the capybara's ears gripping its fur, head tilted slightly as if looking down affectionately, deciding to skip extra accessories like a berry, hat, or scarf to avoid crowding the scene, and keeping the capybara ground-standing without a base.

Now I'm sizing the bird relative to the capybara's head width, making it a plump, whimsical songbird slightly larger than realistic, and working out its body position and radius so its feet sink naturally into the fur at the top of the head.

Next I'm laying out the bird's joint hierarchy—body, head, upper and lower beak—with the body tilted forward at an angle typical of a perched bird, placing each joint's position and aim direction to build a believable pose.

For wings I'm adding a two-joint chain (shoulder and tip) for folded wings, plus a tail chain angled back and slightly upward. Legs get a short joint pair with gripping toes (three forward, one back) positioned to clutch a perch, with the bird's body sitting just above the fur line—something I'll verify visually once rendered.

Now I'm starting the actual build code, defining the capybara's color palette first: warm browns and tans for fur, pink and dark tones for nose and eyes, plus a few extra hues for the bird companion and nearby plants like reeds and daisies.

I'm laying out more head stations toward the cranium and muzzle, then checking how the rounded cap at the nose end affects overall head length relative to body proportions, trying to keep it closer to realistic capybara ratios.

The muzzle should be blocky and deep, so I'll make it taller than wide. For the nose pad, I'll use a surface ray cast from the front to find the exact hit point and place a flattened dark sphere there for the nose detail.

For the nostrils, I'm positioning them using the nose pad's local coordinate frame so they sit on the pad surface, placing them symmetrically at small offsets outward along the pad's normal axis based on its scaled radius.

For the whiskers, I'll sweep thin tubes along simple curves from the muzzle area, using a small radius with enough sides to stay smooth despite the tiny thickness.

For eyes, I'm using surface-ray sampling around the head to locate placement points on the sides near the top, then sticking on glossy black spheres with highlights and a heavy upper lid for that whimsical look.

Actually, simpler than modeling separate lid geometry, I decide to use decals -- projecting an SVG eye texture (including lid, highlight, lashes) directly onto the curved head surface for a cleaner result.

Working out the eyelid geometry...

I'll orient the lid dome so its local +Z aligns with the outward normal and +Y leans toward world up, making it slightly larger than the eyeball and centered on it, using FUR_DARK for a lash-line effect instead of a separate rim piece. Then I'll move on to the ears: small rounded capybara ears at the rear-top of the head, built as extruded rounded semi-ellipse outlines near the base points.

Working through the orientation vectors, I'm leaning toward having the ear plane face sideways with thickness toward the x-axis, tilted slightly outward and up, since that matches how a capybara's small rounded ears sit on the sides of its head.

Adjusting ear geometry orientation...

I'm placing the ear positions at the head's top-rear, checking they clear the bird's wingspan sitting between them, then working out where to position a small daisy accent tucked behind the left ear.

Now I'm constructing the daisy itself as a ring of flattened petal shapes stuck outward from a hit point on the head surface, with a yellow center, figuring out how the ring items should orient so petals face outward correctly.

I'll offset the flower ring off the head along the normal direction using the hit frame. For a whimsical touch I'm considering adding a blade of grass in the mouth and a curved smile line along the muzzle, sweeping it with a catmull curve below the nose.

Now I'm working out the jaw geometry: figuring out where the lower jaw loft sits relative to the head bottom, positioning the jaw joint and chin coordinates so the lower jaw sits flush beneath the head rather than poking out awkwardly.

I'll skip explicitly drawing the mouth line and instead let the seam between the head loft and jaw create a natural shaded crease. For the smile, I'll drape a curve of points along the muzzle's lower cheek area, mirrored on both sides, letting it snap to the nearest surface, then check how it looks before moving on to fur texture cards.

For fur, I'm designing tapered strand textures as small SVGs, tinted by the coat paint, and scattering them as cards across the cheeks, chest, rump, ear fringe, and leg ankles, keeping the total count to a few hundred for a reasonable triangle budget. I'm also defining the body coat paint using layered mottling, grain, and countershading toward the belly color.

I want the back/saddle to darken toward the spine using another countershade layer on top of the base fur, and I'm considering adding tiny whimsical freckles near the muzzle through a custom paint function, though capybaras otherwise have no spots. I'm now working through how to nest a custom head paint function that still references the base coat paint underneath.

For freckles, I'm using a cell-based noise function to pick scattered small dark spots only in the muzzle region, checking cell distance thresholds and hashing cell ids to randomly select which cells get freckled, while restricting to areas where the normal faces outward and forward. I'm also planning a slightly darker ridge along the top of the nose.

Now I'm ready to write the leg geometry, placing front leg roots near the shoulder and defining wrist targets and segment lengths so limbs sprout from inside the body and reach down toward the ground.

Adding toe joints and digit chains...

I'll give toe tips darker blunt nail caps using a color band gradient, with the foot sinking slightly into the floor for contact. Then I'm setting up the hind leg geometry with hip root, ankle target, and a bend hint at the knee, adding a flattened haunch sphere to suggest the thigh muscle bulge.

Now I'm placing the hind foot's three toes with the hock bending backward, adding a small rounded tail stub, and defining the neck joint chain parented to the spine.

Mapping out the spine path from hips through four spans, then continuing the neck curve from its base point upward and forward toward where the head joint will attach.

Placing the head joint just past the neck end with a slight offset to keep the cranium clear of overlap, then adding the jaw joint angled downward and forward for the jaw role. Now defining body loft stations along z from the back to the front, specifying y-height, width, and height values at each station to shape the torso silhouette.

The body bottom sits quite low relative to leg length, so I'm checking whether the belly clearance feels right for a whimsical, stubby-legged capybara look. I'm grouping bones into tail, hips, and spine for the body loft while keeping the neck as a separate chain, and sketching a short tail chain with two joints plus a small stub bump since capybaras barely have tails but the rig still needs something there.

For the neck I'm setting up a sweep with a tapering radius, and adding small anatomical touches like belly fur cards, a chest tuft, and a dark bump on top of the snout to represent the capybara's real-life scent gland for a cute, realistic detail. Now I'm shifting to the bird's joint structure, starting with the bird body attached to the head.

For roles I'm deciding whether duplicate role names (like "head" used for both capybara and bird) cause issues, concluding it should be fine since they belong to separate chains, and planning the bird's lower beak with a "jaw" role. I'm now moving to building the bird's body as a chubby rounded sweep shape.

Writing sweep geometry and paint function...

Now I'm adding the head sphere with the same countershading paint logic for blue back and orange throat, then building the beak as a small cone spike with upper/lower jaw joints.

Adding tiny eyes, crest tufts...

Still shaping wing outline and feather coloring...

Now I'm positioning the wing on a two-joint chain attached at the shoulder, making sure its thickness sits correctly against the body capsule's radius so the inner face nestles just inside the torso surface while the outer face projects outward.

Next I'm building the tail from three fanning feather extrudes behind the body, each a narrow leaf-shaped outline flattened into a horizontal plane with its own length and width, oriented along a back-and-down direction with the fan spread roughly ±12 degrees between feathers.

Then I'm working out tiny leg joints for the bird, placing simple stick bones from body down to a foot position, though I note they'll likely sink into the surrounding fur.

Actually, better to compute the foot height dynamically using a surface ray cast downward at the feet's position, so the bird sits correctly relative to the fur surface rather than using guessed coordinates. I'll derive a base origin for the bird — feet height just below the head's top surface at that location — then define the rest of the bird's body, tail, and legs as relative offsets from that computed base.

I'm working out the body's size and proportions now — a tilted capsule shape stretching from the tail area toward the chest — trying to balance realism against keeping the dimensions small enough to look whimsical rather than overlong.

Total bird length comes out around .2m, with the head sized proportionally and total model height landing near .71m, which feels right. For personality, I want to give the head a slight yaw tilt — like the bird's glancing to one side — to make it feel alive rather than stiff.

Actually, the local coordinate system is based on model directions, not bone-inherited, so applying yaw through the head joint gets complicated with beak geometry following. Simpler idea: skip the tilt and instead make the bird open its beak like it's singing, maybe with little musical notes floating out — that whimsical touch adds more charm than a head tilt would.

For the notes I'd build each as simple extruded shapes: a flattened ellipsoid for the note head, a thin rod for the stem, and a small flag slab, merged together rather than one complex outline polygon.

Now I'm thinking through the capybara's facial expression — half-lidded content eyes with a tiny smile — and need to watch for z-fighting between the fur surface and the eyelids. Then I'll move to writing the actual code, leaving arms and feet groups as optional, and double-check the paint cell types.
